Several open-source CLIs match this description. Most read stdin and write redacted text to stdout, and most cover API keys, emails, and IP addresses.

- **wick** (Go, AGPL-3.0): Detects secrets using bundled Gitleaks-derived rules, plus emails, IP addresses, US phone numbers, and US SSNs. It keeps the structure of JSON, YAML, and .env input. It can also produce reversible tokens. Its docs say it is not a secrets manager. Detects secrets with bundled Gitleaks-derived rules, plus common PII (emails, IP addresses, US phone numbers, US SSNs)
- **leakguard** (Rust, zero-dependency): Redacts emails, credit cards, IPs, JWTs, and API keys from stdin or files. It has a `--check` mode that exits non-zero when sensitive data is found. It also offers several masking styles. `leakguard` CLI -- redact secrets & PII from stdin (or files) and write to stdout.
- **redactcli** (Python, on PyPI): Reads stdin or files and writes redacted output. It also has a scan mode and a GitHub Action. Its README says no cloud, no API key. It targets AWS, GitHub, npm, and other tokens, plus private keys.
- **local-redact** (Python, also runs in the browser): Covers emails, phone numbers, IPs, and API keys, with extra regional IDs such as Gulf and Indian identifiers. It can pipe stdin to stdout and writes a JSON report. Its README notes that Presidio, a well-known alternative, lacks some of those regional IDs.
- **ferret-scan** (Go, single binary): Works offline and scans files or stdin for secrets using entropy analysis and about 40 patterns. It can also redact in a format-preserving way and skips private-range IPs.
- **secret-redactor**: Reads stdin or files and replaces common secrets with a stable marker. It targets JWTs, bearer tokens, PEM keys, credentialed URLs, and emails. Its README is less clear about IP address coverage.

I did not verify licenses, maintenance status, or detection accuracy for most of these. Wick is the only one whose license appeared in the results. For a tool you will trust with real secrets, check the repo's current commits and test it on sample data first.

content.content:
**Install on Linux**

The page doesn't give a Linux-specific procedure. It lists these options:

- `brew install krypsis-io/tap/wick` (the page doesn't say whether this works on Linux)
- `go install github.com/krypsis-io/wick/cmd/wick@latest`
- The install script, `install.sh`, in the repository
- A prebuilt binary from the Releases page, which the page says is available for Linux, macOS, and Windows

**Basic usage (stdin to stdout)**

```
kubectl logs deploy/api | wick
```

wick prints the same text with secrets and personal data replaced. Messages go to stderr, so you can redirect the output, for example `kubectl logs deploy/api | wick | pbcopy`. The page doesn't show a Linux clipboard tool. Other usage: `wick app.log` redacts a file, and `wick app.log > app-safe.log` saves the result. The exit code is 0 if nothing was redacted, 1 if something was, and 2 on error.

**What it detects**

- Known secret formats from the Gitleaks rule set, such as cloud keys, API tokens, private keys, JWTs, and webhook URLs
- Values of keys like `password`, `*_TOKEN`, and `*_SECRET`
- Sensitive HTTP headers such as `Authorization` and `Cookie`
- Passwords in URLs
- All values in Kubernetes Secret `data` and `stringData`
- Personal data: email addresses, IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, US phone numbers, and US Social Security numbers

Detection is rule-based, so formats without a rule (such as internal ticket IDs) aren't found unless you add them in `.wick.yaml`.

**Flags for IPs and emails**

The page doesn't list a flag that targets IPs or emails specifically. Its options are `--dir`, `--out`, `--summary`, `--report`, `--style`, `--format json`, `--tokenize`, `--rehydrate`, `--forget`, and `--token-file`. The config file can turn off built-in rules by ID (`disable_rules`) and allowlist specific values, but the page doesn't list the rule IDs for IP or email detection.

**License**

Apache-2.0. The bundled Gitleaks rules are MIT-licensed, per THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.

**Stars**

1 star, with 0 watchers and 0 forks at the time of capture.

**Latest release date**

Not shown. The Releases section on the page is empty.

**Network calls and telemetry**

The page doesn't mention any network calls or telemetry. It does describe local storage: tokenize mode saves original values in an encrypted token map on disk, and the key is stored in the system keychain (or printed once if no keychain is available). The page doesn't say whether the tool makes any network requests.

I ran one search. None of the results were named "loganon," "logsanitizer" (exact), or "scrub," and the results don't show star counts, so I can't say which tool is the most popular. Here are the closest candidates that match your criteria:

- **LogScrub** (Draylinp/logscrub) is a CLI and browser tool. It swaps IPs, MAC addresses, emails, hostnames, and tokens for numbered placeholders, so the same value gets the same placeholder across a run. It has a `npm`-installable `logscrub` command that reads a file or pipes to stdout. It replaces IPs, MAC addresses, emails, hostnames, passwords and tokens with consistent placeholders.
- **logveil** (PyPI, `logveil-cli`) is a Python CLI that reads streams line by line and works in pipelines. Its docs show piping a command's output into it, and it has an option to keep email addresses. It covers bearer tokens, GitHub and OpenAI-style keys, AWS key IDs, and password assignments.
- **Anonip** (DigitaleGesellschaft/Anonip) is narrower. It only masks the last bits of IPv4 and IPv6 addresses in web server logs, and it can be used with shell redirects.
- **Advanced Log Sanitizer** (MoshikoKar/LogSanitizer) is a GUI app with regex patterns for emails, IPs, and API keys. It doesn't appear to be a pipe-friendly CLI.
- **shush** (adityaarsharma/shush) is a local CLI that replaces IPs, file paths, hostnames, and JWTs with bracketed tags. It's aimed at preparing files for LLMs.

For a pipe-based workflow with token coverage, LogScrub and logveil fit best. Anonip is the choice if you only need IP masking. If you need a specific tool named in your query, such as "loganon," a follow-up search on that name would be needed.

My top pick is **ferret-scan** from AWS Labs ([awslabs/ferret-scan](https://github.com/awslabs/ferret-scan)). It has one gap with IP addresses, and **LogScrub** covers it. I got all of this from the project READMEs and haven't installed or tested either tool. I've assumed you have Python 3 (or Docker) available and are fine with installing something from PyPI or npm.

## Main recommendation: ferret-scan

**Why it fits:**
- It's free and open source (Apache-2.0), and it's the most established option I found: an AWS Labs project with about 100 GitHub stars. Most other tools in this space are small personal projects.
- It works as a filter: it reads stdin, sends the redacted text to stdout, and prints what it found to stderr.
- It runs offline. The README says "No data leaves your host."
- You don't write any regexes. It catches API keys and tokens using 40+ patterns (AWS, GitHub, Stripe, …) plus entropy analysis (spotting random-looking strings), and it also detects emails and IPv4/IPv6 addresses.

**The gap to know about:** It deliberately **skips private IPs** (10.x, 192.168.x and similar ranges) and only flags IPs that appear near keywords that suggest an IP. So it won't catch every IP in a server log. If that matters to you, use LogScrub below as well or instead.

### Install
```bash
# pipx keeps it isolated from system Python
pipx install ferret-scan        # or: pip install --user ferret-scan
# Alternatives:
#   docker pull public.ecr.aws/awslabs/ferret-scan:latest
#   brew tap awslabs/ferret-scan https://github.com/awslabs/ferret-scan && brew install awslabs/ferret-scan/ferret-scan
```

### First run
1. Test it on fake data first:
   ```bash
   printf 'user=alice@example.com ip=203.0.113.7 key=AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE token=ghp_abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789\n' \
     | ferret-scan --stdin --enable-redaction --redaction-strategy simple 2>/dev/null
   ```
   - `--redaction-strategy simple` replaces values with plain placeholders. The other options are `format_preserving` (the default) and `synthetic`, which swaps in fake values.
   - `2>/dev/null` hides the findings report. I couldn't confirm whether that report contains the original secrets, so keep it out of anything you paste.
2. Run it on a real log:
   ```bash
   ferret-scan --stdin --enable-redaction --redaction-strategy simple < server.log 2>/dev/null > server.clean.log
   ```
3. To skip unrelated checks (it runs all 19 by default, including credit cards and SSNs), add `--checks SECRETS,EMAIL,IP_ADDRESS`.

## Alternative or add-on: LogScrub, for full IP coverage

[LogScrub](https://github.com/Draylinp/logscrub) is MIT-licensed and runs locally on Node.js 18.3 or newer.
- It **scrubs all IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, private ones included** (add `--keep-private` if you want to leave those alone).
- It also handles emails, MAC addresses, hostnames, and many token types (AWS, GitHub, GitLab, Slack, Stripe, `sk-` keys, JWTs, `Authorization:` headers, private keys…).
- The same value always gets the same numbered placeholder. That's useful for AI debugging, because "IP_1 failed, then IP_2" still makes sense.
- The downside: it's a one-person project with about 1 star, so expect less vetting.

```bash
npm install -g @draylinp/logscrub
journalctl -u nginx | logscrub --stats > clean.log   # summary goes to stderr
logscrub --check server.log                          # exit code 1 if secrets are found
```

You can also chain the two tools: `ferret-scan --stdin --enable-redaction --redaction-strategy simple < app.log 2>/dev/null | logscrub > clean.log`

## Other options I found but didn't pick
- [wick](https://github.com/krypsis-io/wick): a Go tool that uses Gitleaks' 800+ secret rules plus email and IP detection, so its token coverage is probably the widest. Only about 1 star and no published releases.
- [leakguard](https://docs.rs/crate/leakguard/latest/source/src/bin/leakguard.rs) (Rust) and [redactcli](https://pypi.org/project/redactcli/) / [logveil-cli](https://pypi.org/project/logveil-cli) (Python) are similar small stdin/stdout filters.
- [Anonip](https://github.com/DigitaleGesellschaft/Anonip) only masks IPs.
- Gitleaks and TruffleHog find secrets but don't output a cleaned copy of the text.

## Caveats
- All of these tools match known patterns, so they will miss things: internal hostnames, customer names, and unusual token formats. Look over the output before you paste it.
- If a real secret was ever in a log, rotate it. Redacting it now doesn't help if it was already exposed somewhere else.

Sources:
- [awslabs/ferret-scan](https://github.com/awslabs/ferret-scan) / [fork](https://github.com/orshih6/ferret-scan)
- [Draylinp/logscrub](https://github.com/Draylinp/logscrub)
- [krypsis-io/wick](https://github.com/krypsis-io/wick)
- [leakguard](https://docs.rs/crate/leakguard/latest/source/src/bin/leakguard.rs)
- [redactcli](https://pypi.org/project/redactcli/)
- [logveil-cli](https://pypi.org/project/logveil-cli)
- [local-redact](https://github.com/sumankrsh/local-redact)
- [secret-redactor](https://github.com/nsisongltd/secret-redactor)
- [shush](https://github.com/adityaarsharma/shush)
- [Anonip](https://github.com/DigitaleGesellschaft/Anonip)
